overview: Wuerhosaurus homheni was a large stegosaur from the Early Cretaceous Tugulu Group of Xinjiang, China (~130–120 Ma), notable as one of the last known stegosaurs — most of the family disappeared at the end of the Jurassic, making Wuerhosaurus a rare Cretaceous survivor of this lineage. Its plates are distinctive: low and wide rather than the tall triangular plates of Stegosaurus.

The wide, horizontal plates of Wuerhosaurus have been interpreted as thermoregulatory structures (like a solar panel) rather than display organs, since their low profile reduces visual impact. However, the function of stegosaur plates in all species remains debated, and thermoregulation, display and defence have all been proposed.

fossilSites.name: Tugulu Group
fossilSites.note: Early Cretaceous continental deposits with Wuerhosaurus material — one of the youngest stegosaur records anywhere.

articles.title: Discovery and significance
articles.body: Dong Zhiming described Wuerhosaurus homheni in 1973 from Xinjiang material. Its Early Cretaceous age makes it one of the latest-surviving stegosaurs — most of the family disappears from the fossil record at the Jurassic-Cretaceous boundary (~145 Ma). Wuerhosaurus survived into the Barremian, some 15–20 million years after most of its relatives vanished, as an apparent Cretaceous relict.

articles.title: Plate morphology
articles.body: Unlike the tall pointed or rounded plates of Stegosaurus, Wuerhosaurus plates are described as low and broad with a rounded dorsal margin. This unusual shape may reflect an ecological or thermoregulatory specialisation, though the plates of all stegosaurs are poorly understood functionally. The plates are embedded in skin rather than fused to the skeleton, as in all stegosaurs.

articles.title: Asian stegosaur diversity
articles.body: Asia was a major centre of stegosaur diversity in the Jurassic: Tuojiangosaurus, Huayangosaurus and Chungkingosaurus from China, plus the Indian Dravidosaurus (controversial), represent a rich Asian stegosaur fauna. Wuerhosaurus is thus part of a long Asian stegosaur tradition. Its persistence into the Cretaceous in Asia may reflect the relatively late fauna turnover in this region compared to North America and Europe.

fossilRecord.material: Partial skeletal material including vertebrae, limb bones and plates.
fossilRecord.paleo: Early Cretaceous of central Asia — a rare survival of the stegosaur lineage into the Cretaceous.
fossilRecord.evidence: Stegosaur plates and postcranial anatomy confirm its identity; its Early Cretaceous age makes it one of the last known stegosaurs.

record.mya: exact stage and numerical age unresolved
record.description: Wuerhosaurus homheni was an Early Cretaceous stegosaur from the Tugulu Group of Xinjiang, known from incomplete postcranial remains and distinctive low plate fragments.
facts: No complete skeleton or skull is known for the type species.
The four-tonne point mass is cleared; proposed synonymy with Stegosaurus is not generally accepted.

review.ageReviewNote: The Tugulu Group is Early Cretaceous, but correlations of the relevant unit remain too uncertain to support a narrow stage or numerical age.
residualUncertainty: Species composition, formation age and plate shape remain incompletely known.

evidence.material: Fragmentary postcranial skeletons and isolated plates; skull absent.
evidence.confidenceLimit: Mass and numerical age are cleared; low plate reconstructions are based on incomplete pieces.
evidence.summary: Wuerhosaurus homheni was an Early Cretaceous stegosaur from the Tugulu Group of Xinjiang, known from incomplete postcranial remains and distinctive low plate fragments.
evidence.sourceBasis: Dong (1973), original description of Wuerhosaurus; Maidment et al. (2008), stegosaur systematics
